title: Work Is Sport
why: Meetings, emails and news reports are full of sports images: balls, goalposts, plates and towels. They are quick and vivid, but many come from baseball or cricket, so knowing which side of the Atlantic they belong to helps you choose the right one.
know: drop the ball, move the goalposts, step up to the plate
understand: work as a game with rules, teams and a score
able: Describe a workplace problem or success using sports idioms in a natural, not overdone, way.
Choose a North American or British idiom to suit your listener.
Discuss a song, poem or book that links sport with success, failure or fairness.
mistakes: The ball is on your court now.
The ball is in your court now. It is the tennis court; the ball lands in it.
They keep moving the goalposts. The idiom names the posts themselves.
Can you give me a baseball figure?
Can you give me a ballpark figure? A ballpark is the stadium, so a ballpark figure is roughly in the right area.
He threw the towel after the third rejection.
He threw in the towel. Without in, it only means he threw a towel.
We need to step up to the plate, hit it out of the park, touch base and not drop the ball.
Use one or two at a time. Stacking sports idioms sounds like a parody of corporate jargon.
bigidea: In English, work is often described as a sport: there are players and teams, rules and referees, winners and losers, and a score to keep. A project is a game, a deadline is the final whistle, a mistake is a dropped ball.

The sports chosen tell you where an idiom grew up. North American business talk is full of baseball (ballpark, step up to the plate, out of left field), while British English leans on football and cricket (move the goalposts, a sticky wicket, it's not cricket). Boxing gives everyone below the belt and throw in the towel.
Because sport depends on rules, these idioms are often about fairness. Complaining that someone moved the goalposts or hit below the belt is a moral judgement wrapped in a game image.
hidden: Our team scored a big win with the Quebec contract.
The two firms are neck and neck in the race for the licence.
Let's touch base on Monday about the schedule.
Remote work is a whole new ball game for managers.
She really hit it out of the park with her keynote speech.
Bringing up his divorce in the debate was below the belt.
Changing the deadline without warning? That's just not cricket.
The new director is calling the shots now.

expressions.meaning: make a mistake by failing to do something you were responsible for
expressions.example: Someone dropped the ball and the invoices never went out.
expressions.bend: Tense changes: I dropped the ball on that one. Add the task with on: drop the ball on the renewal.
expressions.note: A soft way to admit a failure, common in North American offices. 'I dropped the ball' sounds more responsible and less dramatic than 'I failed'.

expressions.meaning: a situation where everyone has the same chance
expressions.example: The new rules are meant to create a level playing field for small and large banks.
expressions.bend: Common verbs: create / ensure / provide a level playing field. Opposite: an uneven playing field; verb: level the playing field.
expressions.note: Very common in politics, economics and trade. It is a general sports image, used everywhere in the English-speaking world.

expressions.meaning: unfairly change the rules or targets while something is in progress
expressions.example: Every time we meet the target, head office moves the goalposts.
expressions.bend: Often progressive and a complaint: they keep moving the goalposts. Noun: goalpost-moving.
expressions.note: From British football (soccer). Always critical: it accuses someone of unfairness. Canadians and Americans use it too.

expressions.meaning: it is your turn to act or decide
expressions.example: We've sent our final offer, so the ball's in their court now.
expressions.bend: Change the owner: the ball is in Ottawa's court. Also put the ball back in their court.
expressions.note: From tennis. Use in, not on or at. Often used to show that you have done your part.

expressions.example: I don't need exact numbers, just a ballpark figure for the renovation.
expressions.bend: Also in the ballpark (close enough), in the same ballpark (similar), a ballpark estimate.
expressions.note: From baseball; a ballpark is the stadium. Very North American, but now understood in the UK too. Formal alternative: an approximate figure.

expressions.example: The question about my childhood came completely out of left field.
expressions.bend: Fixed core. Add intensifiers: totally / completely out of left field. Also as adjective: a left-field idea.
expressions.note: Baseball, so mainly North American. British speakers more often say out of the blue. Left-field as an adjective can be positive: unconventional, creative.

expressions.meaning: take responsibility or action when it is needed
expressions.example: When the manager got sick, Priya stepped up to the plate and ran the launch.
expressions.bend: Shortened to step up. Tense and subject change: it's time for the province to step up to the plate.
expressions.note: Baseball: the batter steps up to home plate. A common call to action in politics. British English may prefer rise to the occasion.

expressions.example: After three years of losses, the owners finally threw in the towel and sold the store.
expressions.bend: Word order can change: throw the towel in. Tense changes. Variant: throw in the sponge (old-fashioned).
expressions.note: From boxing: a trainer throws a towel into the ring to stop the fight. Sounds more final and dramatic than give up.

culture.how: The song looks back on a life of struggles and mistakes and turns it into a victory celebration. Because it is played in stadiums after almost every final, it has become the soundtrack for success as winning a trophy, at work as much as in sport.
culture.ask: Why do you think companies and schools love to borrow the language and music of sports victories?

culture.how: A cheerful play-by-play of a hockey game that became a Canadian anthem, played in NHL arenas including Ottawa and Toronto. It shows how one sport can stand for a whole national identity, and why Canadians reach for hockey images (a hat trick, a power play, dropping the gloves) at work.
culture.ask: Which sport supplies the metaphors in your first language? Give one example and translate it for Bill.
culture.find: Stompin' Tom Connors The Hockey Song

culture.how: A small-town baseball team's hopes rest on its star batter, who is so confident that he lets good pitches go by and then strikes out. The comic poem is a classic picture of someone who steps up to the plate and fails through arrogance.
culture.ask: Have you seen a 'Casey' at work: someone talented who lost because of overconfidence?
culture.find: Ernest Thayer Casey at the Bat

culture.how: This non-fiction book (filmed in 2011) follows the Oakland Athletics, a poor baseball team that used statistics to compete with rich clubs. It became a favourite of business readers because it is about finding ways to play on an uneven playing field.
culture.ask: In your field, how could a small player compete with much bigger, richer rivals?

culture.how: Before fighting Sonny Liston for the heavyweight title, Ali (then Cassius Clay) became famous for rhyming boasts. His best-known slogan, usually credited to his assistant Drew Bundini Brown, compared his light footwork to a butterfly and his punches to a bee's sting. Sport talk itself runs on metaphor.
culture.ask: Is confident self-promotion admired or disliked where you grew up? Would Ali's style work in a job interview?
culture.find: Muhammad Ali butterfly bee slogan 1964 Liston

match.r: fail to do something you were responsible for
match.why: A player who drops the ball loses it for the team.
On a flat field, neither team has a slope in its favour.
If the goal moves during the game, you can never score.
In tennis, you must hit the ball once it lands on your side.
It's in the ballpark: in the right area, but not exact.
Something arrives from a direction you weren't watching.
In baseball the batter steps up to the plate to face the pitch.
A boxer's corner throws in the towel to end the fight.

sort.h: Where does each idiom come from? Sort them into baseball, boxing or football and cricket.

items.why: A ballpark is a baseball stadium.
Left field is part of a baseball diamond.
The batter steps up to home plate.
Runners touch each base in baseball.

items.w: hit it out of the park
items.why: A home run leaves the ballpark completely.
A trainer throws a towel into the ring to stop a fight.
Boxing rules forbid punches below the belt.
A boxer pushed against the ropes is close to losing.
Goalposts belong to football (soccer) and rugby; the idiom is British.
Cricket stands for fair play in British English.
A wet cricket pitch made batting hard, so a sticky wicket is a tricky situation.

pick.q: I was supposed to book the venue, but I completely ___. It's gone.
pick.why: Failing to do a task you were responsible for is dropping the ball.

pick.q: Small farms want ___ with the big agribusinesses when it comes to subsidies.
pick.why: They want equal chances: a level playing field.

pick.q: We hit last year's sales target, and now they say we need 20 percent more just to get a bonus. They're ___.
pick.why: Changing the target unfairly is moving the goalposts.

pick.q: We've answered all their questions and lowered our price. ___ now.
pick.why: We have done our part; it's their turn to decide.

pick.q: I won't hold you to it, but can you give me ___ for the new roof?
pick.why: A rough estimate is a ballpark figure.

pick.q: Her resignation came ___. Nobody in the office suspected anything.
pick.why: Totally unexpected: out of left field.

pick.q: With the deadline tomorrow and half the team sick, we need someone to ___.
pick.why: Taking responsibility in a crisis is stepping up to the plate.

pick.q: After two failed appeals, the family finally ___ and accepted the ruling.
pick.why: Giving up after a long fight is throwing in the towel.

spot.q: I've sent my proposal, so the ball is on your court.
spot.why: The ball lands in a tennis court, so the idiom uses in.

spot.q: The government keeps moving the goals on emissions targets.
spot.why: The fixed idiom names the goalposts.

spot.q: Can you give me a baseball figure for the catering?
spot.why: A ballpark figure is a rough estimate. The idiom names the stadium, not the sport.

spot.q: After the third rejection letter, he threw the towel and stopped applying.
spot.why: The particle in is essential: throw in the towel (or throw the towel in).

spot.q: Mentioning her illness in the debate was really under the belt.
spot.why: Unfair attacks are below the belt. Under your belt means experience you already have.

type.q: Sorry, I dropped the ___ on your reference letter. I'll send it tonight.
type.why: Drop the ball = fail to do something you were responsible for.

type.q: The trade deal is meant to level the playing ___ for Canadian exporters.
type.why: Level the playing field = make the chances equal.

type.q: Every time I finish the report, my manager moves the ___.
type.why: Move the goalposts = unfairly change the target.

type.q: That idea came out of left ___, but it might actually work.
It's time for the big tech firms to step up to the ___ on privacy.
type.why: Step up to the plate = take responsibility.

type.q: Working from home with three kids is a whole new ball ___.
type.why: A whole new ball game = a completely different situation.

bend.q: Which version sounds natural after a mistake at work? ___
opts: I really dropped the ball on that client.
I really dropped a ball for that client.
I really let the ball drop on that client.
bend.why: Drop the ball keeps the and takes on + task. A ball or let the ball drop sound like literal sport.

bend.q: Which version sounds natural in a trade negotiation? ___
opts: The ball is now on Washington's court.
The ball is now firmly in Washington's court.
bend.why: You can add firmly and change the owner, but keep in + court.

bend.q: Which version sounds natural about an estimate? ___
opts: Your guess is in the same ballpark as mine.
Your guess is in the same baseball as mine.
Your guess is the same ballpark figure of mine.
bend.why: In the same ballpark = similar. It is a common, natural variation.

bend.q: Which version sounds natural for a business story? ___
opts: The startup threw its towel at the market.
The startup was towel-thrown in the end.
The startup threw the towel in after two years.
bend.why: The particle can move: throw the towel in. Passive or other changes break the idiom.

talk: Tell Bill about a time someone moved the goalposts on you at work or school. How did you react?
Role-play: you are a manager. A team member has dropped the ball on an important task. Talk to them firmly but kindly.
Stompin' Tom made hockey sound like Canada's national story. Which sport tells the story of your country, and what metaphors come from it?
Is the job market in your field a level playing field? Who has an advantage, and why?
Which sports idioms do you find useful, and which sound like empty corporate jargon to you? Give examples.

match.r: make brief contact to check in
match.why: A baseball runner touches each base on the way round.
When the game changes, the old rules and strategies no longer apply.

match.l: hit it out of the park
match.why: A home run that leaves the stadium is the best possible hit.
Hitting below the belt is against boxing rules.
Cricket stood for gentlemanly fair play.
A boxer trapped against the ropes is in trouble.

pick.q: Let's ___ next week and see how the hiring is going.
pick.why: A short check-in is touching base.

pick.q: Her presentation to the investors was brilliant. She ___.
opts: hit it out of the park
pick.why: Doing something extremely well is hitting it out of the park.

pick.q: Joking about his stutter during the interview was ___.
pick.why: A cruel, unfair remark is below the belt.

pick.q: Managing a team of forty after leading a team of four is ___.
pick.why: A completely different situation is a whole new ball game.

pick.q: After the scandal, the party was ___ and its poll numbers kept falling.
pick.why: Close to defeat is on the ropes.

pick.q: When the chair resigned, the deputy ___ and kept the board together.
pick.why: She took responsibility in a crisis: she stepped up to the plate.

spot.q: Let's touch the base after lunch about the budget.
Making us reapply after we were already accepted? That's not tennis.
spot.why: The British idiom for unfairness is it's not cricket.

spot.q: Her question came out of right field and nobody knew how to answer.
spot.why: The fixed idiom is out of left field.

spot.q: With two new hires, our department is finally stepping up to the plateau.
spot.why: Step up to the plate (the batter's home plate). A plateau is flat high ground.

type.q: My boss wants a ___ figure for the trip by Friday.
type.why: A ballpark figure = a rough estimate. Rough or approximate also works, but ballpark is the idiom.

type.q: The candidates traded blows, and some of them landed below the ___.
type.why: Below the belt = unfair or cruel.

type.q: I'll touch ___ with the supplier this afternoon.
The ball is in the union's ___ now.
type.why: The ball is in your court = it's your turn to act.

type.q: After losing two major clients, the agency is on the ___.
type.why: On the ropes = close to defeat, like a boxer. On the rocks (in serious trouble) also fits.

type.q: Don't throw in the ___ yet; we still have a week.
type.why: Throw in the towel = give up.

bank.q: The shipping team ___ and the parts arrived a week late.
opts: hit it out of the park
bank.why: Failing in a responsibility is dropping the ball.

bank.q: International students say high fees mean there's no ___ for them.
bank.why: Equal chances for all: a level playing field.

bank.q: First they asked for two references, now they want five. They keep ___.
bank.why: Changing requirements unfairly is moving the goalposts.
I have done my part; it's her turn to act.

bank.q: The plumber gave us ___ of about two thousand dollars.
bank.why: A rough estimate is a ballpark figure.

bank.q: The CEO's sudden support for a four-day week came ___.
bank.why: Unexpected: out of left field.

bank.q: When the volunteers quit, local businesses ___ and funded the festival.
bank.why: They took responsibility when it was needed.

bank.q: After a decade of falling sales, the newspaper ___ and stopped printing.
bank.why: Giving up is throwing in the towel.

bank.q: Her pitch to the Dragons really hit it out of the ___.
bank.why: Hit it out of the park = do something extremely well.

bank.q: Getting the minister on the phone is a sticky ___.
bank.why: A sticky wicket (British, cricket) = a difficult situation.

bank.q: Insulting his family was below the ___.
bank.why: Below the belt = unfair and hurtful.

bank.q: The new director is calling the ___ now.
bank.why: Call the shots = be the one who makes decisions.

bank.q: Once the twins arrived, travel became a whole new ball ___.
bank.why: A whole new ball game = a completely different situation.

bank.q: We need someone to step up the plate and lead the project.
bank.why: The batter steps up to the plate; to is needed.

bank.q: The team leader dropped a ball on the safety training.
bank.why: The idiom uses the: drop the ball.

bank.q: Can we touch base tomorrow morning about the budget?
bank.why: Correct! Touch base = a short check-in, very common in North American offices.

bank.q: The new tax rules are supposed to level the playing field.
bank.why: Correct! Level the playing field = make chances equal.

bank.a: The ball is in their court now.
alt: The ball is now in their court.
Now the ball is in their court.
bank.why: The ball is in their court = it's their turn to act.

bank.a: Our team really hit it out of the park.
bank.why: Subject + really + hit it out of the park.

bank.a: Please give me a ballpark figure by Friday.
alt: Give me a ballpark figure by Friday please.
bank.why: Give me + a ballpark figure + time phrase.
